relevant_group_routes.relationship: National consensus in Canadian and US historiography
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, p. 5) calls the pre-1960s Canadian approach "similar to that of the consensus school in the United States": minimizing internal divisions and stressing what united Canadians. Davis (1985, p. 102) likewise says Careless's metropolitan interpretation "fits the mould of 'consensus' history". Comparison with the consensus half of the atlas entry only. Careless's 1954 article, read for revision 1.136, criticises the Canadian historians who adapted Turner's frontier thesis; that critique is the separate edge from his person entry (j_m_s_careless → progressive), not this comparison.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Urban history rejects the metropolitan thesis
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Davis (1985, abstract): metropolitan theses are several rather than one; their indeterminacy about relations between classes is why urban historians "feraient mieux d'abandonner complètement l'approche métropolitaine". Targets the metropolitan strand only, not the staple approach or national synthesis.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Metropolitanism: Canadian history read through metropolitan centres that organize frontiers and hinterlands, proposed as a wider framework than the frontier-environmentalist reading (1954)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History', Canadian Historical Review 35:1 (1954), pp. 1–21, read in full in an Internet Archive scan of the issue. He sorts English-Canadian historiography into 'schools', 'merely for convenience' (p. 2): a Britannic school, a School of Political Nationhood, and 'the Environmentalist School, or North Americans All', which 'built particularly on the concept of the frontier in North American history derived from Turner' (p. 5); he names Munro, Underhill, Sage, Lower, Landon, A. S. Morton and A. L. Burt, adding that 'no tight determinism is intended in thus naming these authors, nor, on the whole, did they display any' (p. 6, n. 6). He finds in them 'a certain tendency to fix values', so that western farmers were 'Good' and eastern business men 'Evil' (p. 12), and 'a tendency to overvalue the influence of native North American forces and the material environment, and a tendency to undervalue forces transferred from Europe and the non-material environment' (pp. 13–14); 'while in no way underrating the very great contributions which frontierism and environmentalism have made', it 'does seem necessary to look for a wider framework' (p. 14). The Laurentian school of Innis and Creighton offered 'a metropolitan rather than a frontier viewpoint', and 'The result was virtually to establish “metropolitanism” in Canadian historiography' (p. 16). The metropolis is 'a city of outstanding size' dominating 'other cities and their countrysides, the whole area being organized by the metropolis, through control of communications, trade, and finance, into one economic and social unit' (p. 17), in 'almost a feudal chain of vassalage' (p. 17); 'the rise of metropolitanism is the other side of the coin to frontier expansion' (p. 18). His examples include the Clear Grits organized around Toronto, the Globe and George Brown (p. 19). He limits the claim: 'if we reject a frontier determinism we should hardly replace it with a metropolitan determinism' (p. 19), and concedes that a metropolitan interpretation may 'only restate old problems in somewhat different terms. It may be so: but what is particularly needed is a restatement' (p. 21). A contribution, not a founding: he credits Lower's Colony to Nation and essays, Masters's The Rise of Toronto (1947) and its source in Gras (p. 17, nn. 30–31), and the Laurentian school (p. 16). In-period reception and criticism, from Donald F. Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), pp. 95–113, read in full: the article 'heralded the arrival of “metropolitanism” as a “vitalizing approach”'; 'few other journal articles have been more widely cited or more frequently quoted' (p. 95); for most historians it became, in Carl Berger's words as Davis quotes them, 'the programmatic statement of the metropolitan approach' (pp. 95–96). Davis quotes W. L. Morton's objection that the metropolitan thesis, 'which he associated with both Creighton and Careless', 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (p. 98), and S. D. Clark's at the 1974 CHA meeting that 'it serves no useful purpose to work with such categories or concepts as metropolis and hinterland when what is metropolis can also be considered hinterland' (p. 107); both are quoted-in witnesses, not read here. Davis's own judgment: Careless, combining Gras's ecological model with the Laurentian school's elites, 'has produced a relatively sterile hybrid', 'of only limited usefulness in guiding research' (p. 102); his interpretation 'fits the mould of “consensus” history' (p. 102); 'the Gras-Careless statement of metropolitanism is weak on causality; it is more taxonomic than explanatory' (p. 103). Davis also reports that Careless disclaimed 'such a metropolitan “thesis”' in 1973 while keeping the 'approach' (p. 96, quoting Acadiensis 3, 1973). edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition) stays: it records the urban historians' critique at group level.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, and the frontierism Canadian historians took from it, criticised as environmental determinism; the frontier recast as a dependent of the metropolis (1954)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954), read in full. He summarises Turner's thesis that 'the greatest formative influence' in American history had been 'the open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6) and judges: 'This was environmental determinism at its most forthright. The wilderness and the men it produced had made America' (p. 7). Against it he sets the metropolitan reading: the frontier's culture 'originally stems from a metropolitan community; at root, learning and ideas radiate from there—and thus is Turner answered' (p. 18); 'the frontier, far from being essentially independent and self-reliant, is in the largest sense a dependent' (p. 18); and 'the functioning of metropolitanism may do more to explain the course of Canadian history than concepts of frontierism borrowed from the United States and set forth before the significance of the modern metropolis was clear' (p. 20). 'At any rate, frontierism, along with earlier schools and approaches, has had its use and its day' (p. 21). His qualifications are kept: 'Defenders of Turner might claim that he had not proposed a frontier hypothesis as the only key to American history' (p. 7); the frontier thesis 'proper' was never 'adopted as fully or dogmatically in Canada as it was in the United States—and there, of course, it has long been the subject of qualification and criticism' (p. 1); Canadian environmentalists took over 'the general approach and mood of Turner and company ... rather than the precise frontier thesis, which received little direct application in Canada' (p. 6). He draws on American critics of Turner (Hayes, Fox, Schlesinger Jr.; pp. 7–8) and on Canadian ones (McDougall 1929, Stanley 1940; p. 10, n. 21). The critique is therefore aimed at Turner's thesis and above all at its Canadian adaptation; the Canadian historians he names sit in cdn_national_tradition and are covered by edge 1. In-period reading: Davis (1985, p. 95, read) calls the article 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'. Davis (p. 109) also quotes Careless on television saying of Turner's thesis that 'like any view of history which gets oversimplified, overpopularized, it becomes untrue; it becomes a myth' (undated, a quoted-in witness). No reply by a Turnerian historian was found or read.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The metropolis–hinterland approach, taken up by Canadian urban historians in the 1970s and then contested by them (1954–85)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own statements. The 1954 article proposes the metropolis and its hinterland as a field of study, including 'social and cultural associations' as well as economic ties (pp. 17–18), and names Masters's The Rise of Toronto as the closest application (p. 17). In 1981 he writes that 'urban history' grew within regional writing because cities 'are also centres that focus and structure regions or sub-regions about them. The interplay of city and region thus demands and has received attention', and that he had 'always sought to emphasize the reciprocal and complementary nature of the relations between the great city and the territory it dominates' (Manitoba History no. 1, web text). Davis (1985) lists his urban-history articles: 'Urban Development in Canada', Urban History Review 1 (1974), and 'Metropolis and Region', Urban History Review 3 (1979) (nn. 6, 11; unread). In-period reception, from Davis, Urban History Review 14:2 (1985), read in full: 'In the 1970s metropolitanism helped preside over the birth of a new sub-discipline, urban history', and according to Artibise and Linteau (1984) the articles by Careless on metropolis and region 'marked, in some ways at least, the self-conscious beginning of urban history' in Canada (p. 96; a quoted-in witness); urban historians 'have remained the most faithful to the metropolitan concept of J.M.S. Careless, the godfather of their subdiscipline' (p. 96); Gilbert Stelter called the metropolitan thesis in 1977 'the most significant approach to Canadian urban history' (p. 96, quoted). A contribution, contested within the field: Davis argues that 'there is no single metropolitan thesis' (p. 107), that Careless's approach 'has fallen into desuetude in historical circles' (p. 103), that Artibise found the metropolis/hinterland concept 'not really a theory that explain[ed] Canadian urban development' (p. 103, quoted), and that urban historians 'might do better by abandoning the metropolitan approach altogether' (abstract, p. 95). Davis also records Careless's own reserve: he would 'disclaim and deny such a metropolitan “thesis”' (p. 96, quoting 1973). This is a Canadian contribution; it does not claim that Dyos's or US urban history drew on Careless. edge_800 (urbanhistory → cdn_national_tradition, critique) stays: it records the field's rejection of metropolitanism, this edge the field's use of it.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Metropolis and hinterland in Canadian urban history, 1954–85

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The Laurentian narrative: the St. Lawrence commercial system as the basis of a transcontinental Canada (1937), carried through Dominion of the North (1944) and the Macdonald biography (1952–55)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, his own text. Dominion of the North (1944; pages read in an open copy): the post at Quebec gave the French 'the one great river system which led to the Atlantic seaboard from the heart of the continent'; 'Inevitably the river came to seem the natural basis of a great commercial empire stretching far into the distant west; and the achievement of this empire became the common objective of successive generations of Canadians, though their methods altered and the staple products of their trade were sometimes changed. The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur' (p. 21); the rivalry of 'the northern and southern routes, between Montreal and New York, for the control of the Great Lakes system and the command of the western trade', a conflict that 'was to remain essentially the same' (pp. 24–25); 'Quebec had been the origin of the empire of the St. Lawrence; it was to be the genesis of the Dominion of Canada' (p. 298). In-period reception. Herbert Heaton's review (CJEPS, 1938; first page, p. 565, read) quotes the book as 'an attempt to trace the relations between the commercial system of the St. Lawrence and the political development of Canada' (the book's words as Heaton quotes them; the 1937 book is unread) and reads it as a test of the economic interpretation of history that 'has pleased neither the Marxians nor their enemies'. Michel Brunet (RHAF, 1953, p. 579) calls him 'l'un des maîtres contemporains de l'historiographie anglo-canadienne'; Guy Frégault (RHAF, 1955, p. 446) sums up the Macdonald biography as 'Nationalisme antiaméricain, impérialisme et centralisation : synthèse canadienne, — je veux dire anglo-canadienne'. His own retrospect, 1969 (read in full; a later statement by the author, not evidence of what the 1937 book says): 'This Laurentian theme has its basis in the fact that the St. Lawrence is the one great river system that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent of North America'; the river 'has inspired generations of Canadians to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior of the continent' (p. 16); 'The west, it was believed, would make Canada a nation, and the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); in choosing Macdonald he had 'stumbled upon the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase', so that he had written 'a trilogy on one theme' (p. 16). The phrase, he says, came to be regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea' (p. 14). Later readings: Ouellet (1984, pp. 226–227) calls him 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; Salmon (1997) says he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. Contested in period: Brunet found French-Canadian newspapers unread ('Il n'a pas jugé nécessaire de dépouiller un seul journal canadien-français', p. 580) and 'nombreux préjugés' (p. 581); Frégault asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ? Tout simplement, ils n'y sont pas' (p. 447), while praising the work as 'fondé sur une compréhension exacte de l'histoire du Canada' (p. 444); W. L. Morton, as quoted by Davis (1985), saw in Creighton 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played' (Davis, p. 97) and held that the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (Davis, p. 98); the critic George Woodcock (1979, p. 140) called his treatment of Confederation as centralist 'a major distortion'. A contribution, not a founding.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Innis's staple studies as a resource for Creighton's Laurentian narrative, as Creighton's own staple vocabulary and later readers show; Creighton rejected the story that the 1937 book grew from their friendship
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own texts. Dominion of the North (1944) frames the St. Lawrence system by its staples ('The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur', p. 21), and its reading list (pp. 505–507) names Innis's The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940). The 1957 presidential address recalls 'the 1930's, when the influence of Harold Innis was at its height and everybody was writing and talking about staple production' (p. 3), and exempts Innis from the Marxian fashion: 'most of the professional economists — and especially Innis — refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6). In 1957 he also published Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (unread); Benoît Brouillette's review (1957, p. 529, read) reports Creighton's account of Innis's Canada as an east–west system 'marqué par le Saint-Laurent et les Grands-Lacs', at once 'transocéanique et transcontinental'. The qualification, his own (1969, pp. 14–15): 'The Empire of the St. Lawrence, it is sometimes confidently asserted, was the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis ... These explanations, like most simple generalizations, happen to be wrong'; the subject was suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy', and he was 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence' about the Montreal merchants (p. 16). Readers: George Woodcock (1979, p. 134): 'Creighton's master was H. A. Innis, especially the Innis of The Fur Trade in Canada, which contained the essential germ out of which — with Innis's encouragement — Creighton built the scenario of his first book'; Fernand Ouellet (1984, p. 226): Creighton started 'partant de la théorie des staples'; Deborah Harrison (1981), as quoted by Davis (1985, p. 97): 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Salmon (1997): he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. The edge records Innis's work as a resource the Laurentian narrative used, not a teacher–pupil derivation; Creighton's denial concerns the origin of the subject, not the use of the staple framework.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Staples behind the Laurentian narrative, contested

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, as taken up by Canadian historians in the 1930s and 1940s, rejected as an imported 'continental revelation' that Canadian history would not fit (1957)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own text, the 1957 CHA presidential address (read in full). Canadian historians had 'accepted, for historical purposes, the two highly fashionable political theories which dominated the thought of the inter-war and war years': 'the Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'the Frontier Theory' (p. 6). Of the second: 'Turner ... fixed upon the movement of settlement across the continent as the most important fact in its history'; 'the source of creative inspiration and action was found not at the centre, but at the periphery, of western culture' (p. 8). Applied to Canada, 'painful difficulties were immediately encountered': the frontier's progress 'had been evidently modified by all sorts of extraneous and unnatural things such as railways, efficient police, governmental supervision'; in 1837 'the rebels had come, not from the frontier, but from the older settled parts of the province'; yet its believers 'kept insisting that Canadian democracy was "forest-born"' (p. 9). He ends: historians bought 'a couple of suits of imported intellectual reach-me-downs' and a new generation would show 'less deference for imported theories of historical change and more respect for the manifold facts of Canadian experience' (p. 12). The critique inverts his own Laurentian premise, that change radiates from the centre. Limits: the address is a polemic and names no Canadian frontierist; Turner is not quoted beyond the phrases Creighton cites, and the atlas's own reading of Turner (progressive/multiple_hypotheses) shows him advocating multiple hypotheses rather than a single doctrine. Context: Careless's 1954 CHR article, unread here, was 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (Davis 1985, p. 95). No in-period reply to the address was looked for.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: A call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ and ‘the significance of the sexes, of gender groups’, quoted by Joan Scott as an early relational use of gender (1975–76; Scott 1986)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: A reader’s explicit claim, read. Scott, ‘Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis’, AHR 91:5 (1986), p. 1054: those who wanted ‘a relational notion’ used ‘gender’; ‘Thus Natalie Davis suggested in 1975, “It seems to me that we should be interested in the history of both women and men, that we should not be working only on the subjected sex any more than an historian of class can focus entirely on peasants. Our goal is to understand the significance of the sexes, of gender groups in the historical past.”’ (n. 4, citing Feminist Studies 3, Winter 1975–76, p. 90). Davis’s 1976 article is unread; her words are as Scott quotes them. Her own retrospect (1997, p. 16, read) describes the same programme: ‘examining the range of relations between and concepts about women and men in different times and places’. The Holberg committee (2010, read): ‘Her work brings gender to the fore’. A precursor statement taken up in Scott’s argument, not a claim that Davis founded gender history or shared Scott’s later theoretical position.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Festive misrule and religious riot read as culturally patterned action, with violence ‘related here less to the pathological than to the normal’ (1971–75)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own text. ‘The Rites of Violence’ (Past & Present 59, 1973; pp. 52–53, 57, 60–61 and 90–91 read): violence is explained ‘in terms of the goals of their actions and in terms of the rôles and patterns of behaviour allowed by their culture. Religious violence is related here less to the pathological than to the normal’; it had ‘a connection in time, place and form with the life of worship’ (p. 90); crowd violence has ‘some structure to it — here dramatic and ritual’ (p. 91). She sets this against Estèbe’s appeal to the ‘collective unconscious’ (p. 90). Her retrospect (1997, read): ‘The Reasons of Misrule’ began in 1969 from Van Gennep and Bakhtin (pp. 13–14); the title Society and Culture (1975) ‘seemed quite fresh and anthropological at the time’ (p. 15). Reception: Hunt’s New Cultural History (1989) makes ‘Thompson and Davis’ one of its models for cultural history in Desan’s chapter (publisher contents; chapter unread), and the graph’s earlier reading of Hunt’s introduction records her among its formative resources. Holberg committee (2010); Hesse (2024): ‘methodologically heterodox, incorporating anthropological and literary approaches’. Estèbe’s 1975 comment on ‘Rites’ and Davis’s rejoinder (Past & Present 67) are unread.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Her study of French youth abbeys and charivaris used by Thompson as ‘une étude importante’ in his essay on English rough music (1971–72)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Thompson’s own text, read in excerpts. ‘« Rough Music » : le charivari anglais’, Annales ESC 27 (1972), in the 2020 Socio-anthropologie reprint (paragraph numbers; no Annales pages): ‘Dans une étude importante, Natalie Davis a examiné certains aspects du charivari en France au xvie siècle’ (¶36); he uses her findings on the kinds of charivari and the ‘quasi-institutionalised’ role of youth abbeys, citing ‘The Reasons of Misrule’ (Past and Present 50, 1971, pp. 41–75; n. 40), with further uses at nn. 51 and 59. He reads her as following Lévi-Strauss on ‘la masse de jeunes disponibles’ (¶48), which is his characterisation. Walsham (2017; opening extract read) calls the two essays ‘classics of twentieth-century historical writing’ and edits their letters of 1970–72 (unread). Hunt’s volume (1989) pairs them as a model for cultural history (Desan; chapter unread).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Finlay charges an ‘excess of invention’ against ‘the sovereignty of the sources’ in her Bertrande de Rols; Davis answers that where reconstruction stops and invention begins was ‘precisely the question’ the book posed (1988)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: This arrow represents Robert Finlay’s intervention in the debate over evidence in microhistory (micro/reconstruction_invention), not a verdict of the field. Finlay, AHR 93:3 (1988), 553–571, read in full: ‘Davis fails to show that her view of women in peasant society is relevant to the case she is examining’ (p. 557); ‘self-fashioning’ ‘is merely imposed on the historical record as an ingenious assertion’ (p. 564); ‘If historical records can be bypassed so thoroughly in the service of an inventive blend of intuition and assertion, it is difficult to see what distinguishes the writing of history from that of fiction’ (p. 569); ‘speculation, whether founded on intuition or on concepts drawn from anthropology and literary criticism, is supposed to give way before the sovereignty of the sources … Davis has permitted an excess of invention’ (p. 571). He praises ‘its eloquent portrait of peasant life … its emphasis on the central role of women’ (p. 569). Davis, ‘On the Lame’, AHR 93:3 (1988), 572–603, read in part: the question ‘is precisely the question I hoped readers would ask and reflect on’; she would have preferred a critique ‘more subject to “the sovereignty of sources” to which it claims loyalty’ (p. 572); ‘he plays Savonarola to my Montaigne. Fortunately, historical practice can profit from each stance’ (p. 574); ‘proto-feminist’ is ‘a careless reporting of my text’ (p. 584). The group endpoint locates Finlay’s critique within the debate over microhistorical reconstruction; it does not assign him membership in a school. Ginzburg’s 1984 postface to the Italian edition, cited by Finlay (p. 569 n. 71), is unread.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: A narrative of four charivaris cited by Stone among works turning to narrative, after she criticised his draft (1979); later, pardon tales read as crafted stories without discrediting the archives (1987)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Stone, Past & Present 85 (1979), read: p. 3, starred note, thanks ‘Natalie Davis’ among colleagues ‘for valuable criticism of an early draft of this paper’; p. 18: ‘Natalie Davis has presented a narrative of four charivaris or ritual public shame procedures in seventeenth-century Lyon and Geneva, in order to illustrate community efforts to enforce public standards of honour and propriety’ (n. 29, the essay forthcoming in Le Goff and Schmitt, Le charivari). Her own account (1997, p. 21, read): she called her 1987 book Fiction in the Archives ‘somewhat to the consternation of Lawrence Stone to whom it was dedicated’; ‘“fiction” referred not to falsification, but to the crafting element in everything we do and say. Rather than being on an extreme anti-foundationalist mission to discredit the archives, I was presenting them as a source of new evidence’. As the revival scope requires, being named by Stone does not imply that she accepted his diagnosis. Fiction in the Archives is unread.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Charivari narrative; Fiction in the Archives, 1979–87

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Decentred comparison: European women’s lives set beside colonial domination and non-European respondents (1995), a Muslim traveller between worlds (2006), and a programme of ‘decentering history’ (2010)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own retrospect (1997, read): Women on the Margins was to ‘expand the single microhistory into a decentered comparison of three European lives’ (p. 21); she asked about ‘the uninvited French intrusion into the American woodlands’ and Merian’s ‘African and Indian slaves’ (p. 22), introduced ‘non-European women … not just as silent objects … but as active respondents’ (p. 22), and felt ‘permanently relocated as an historian of Europe’, with a new project on ‘cultural mixture’ along ‘the caravan routes of North Africa’ (p. 23). The conclusion of Women on the Margins (davis_margins_primary, earlier reading) shows marginality coexisting with colonial domination. Holberg committee (2010, read): ‘connecting early modern Europe with new areas of comparative history, exploring cultural, geographical and religious interchange’; Women on the Margins and Trickster Travels explore ‘the translation and transmission of cultures’. ‘Decentering History’ (Holberg Symposium, 2010; abstract only) moves ‘beyond a focus on Europe or the West’. Hesse (2024): ‘there were no dark parts of the globe’. Trickster Travels (2006) and the 2011 article are unread. Subrahmanyam’s mediated link from Kafadar to Davis (1997) stays on edge_641.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Scott recalls first hearing “gender” used in a paper by Davis at the Berkshire Conferences of the 1970s (2008); her 1986 essay had quoted Davis’s call to study the significance of the sexes
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Scott's own acknowledgement, read in full in the authorised Spanish translation of "Unanswered Questions" (AHR 113:5, 2008; Debate Feminista 40, 2009, p. 101): "Ahí escuché por primera vez que se mencionaba el género; fue en una ponencia de Natalie Zemon Davis" (citing Davis 1976: 90). English renderings are atlas translations from Spanish. Scott sets her own limit on the same page: "yo no fui el origen del concepto de género, ni siquiera entre las historiadoras", and names a second, literary source in her Brown colleagues of the early 1980s. The 1986 quotation of Davis (p. 1054, n. 4) is the existing reading behind edge_1029, which records Davis's contribution to gender history as a field; this edge records Scott's acknowledged personal debt, with the 2008 recollection as new evidence. Not a claim that Davis shared Scott's later theoretical position.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Davis and Scott’s first hearing of gender, 1970s–2008

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Ginzburg cites Davis’s charivari research as an exemplary use of indirect evidence for popular culture.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Preface to the Italian edition, English translation p. xvii. This records an explicitly praised methodological example in Ginzburg’s own argument. It does not claim that the cited scholar founded his practice, supplied the entire book’s method or endorsed Ginzburg. John and Anne Tedeschi’s translation and the 1976/1980/1992 distinction remain; the cited scholars’ complete works are not newly read.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Davis praises The Birth of Purgatory but asks for more rigorous causal links between its cultural parallels, especially cartography and judicial practice (1985).
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her signed review accepts converging evidence for some arguments while distinguishing asserted affinities from demonstrated connections. It questions the birth metaphor without rejecting the book’s achievement. Review of Goldhammer’s 1984 translation; monograph unread.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: In her 2013 foreword, Davis treats Farge’s account of archival work as a guide that deepens her own understanding of research, interpretation and the material encounter with documents.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Davis’s own selected foreword, especially xii–xv, not evidence of formative influence on her earlier career. Her coediting recollection on x establishes collaboration without causal priority. Thomas Scott-Railton translated Farge’s 1989 book; Davis wrote the separate 2013 foreword. The legal preview ends during xv; the complete foreword and Farge’s book body remain unread.

existing_claim_assessment: Both actual incident claims, the roster and two David-specific source qualifications inspected. All 32 candidate surname group routes map to five other Davis identities. All 57 source catalogue records screened for relevance; 55 attach to false-positive routes and are not promoted as David evidence. Preserve all old claims and qualifications; this is not fresh verification of those 55 originals.

coverage.resources: Genovese through Davis and named Sinha; Hofstadter through Epps; Weber/Gramsci through Sinha; Stampp and other mentors held for absent endpoints. Freud through Erikson is explicitly mediated by Sinha p. 151; direct Freud reading is not claimed.
coverage.criticism: Davis disputes Williams’s economic decline hypothesis, with Solow’s defense retained; Davis criticizes Genovese’s politics; Foner questions Davis’s psychology against fugitive evidence. Sinha, Epps and Haskell critical leads remain explicit.
coverage.reception: Faust’s first-person generational debt retains the plural cohort; no student or sole-source claim. Elkins psychological analogy, Finley’s qualified exchange, and Plumb/Knight/Grimsted/Temperley social-background criticism receive explicit absent-endpoint holds.
coverage.remaining_limits: Selected passages only; full trilogy, 1969 book, named theoretical originals and debate originals unread. Mediation explicit; no quota or exhaustive-network claim.
